title: Owners, sudo and umask
summary: Who owns a file, how to act as root safely, and why new files start as 644.

steps.title: Users, groups, chown
body: ```text
$ id
uid=1000(ana) gid=1000(ana) groups=1000(ana),27(sudo),998(docker)
- Users are listed in `/etc/passwd`, groups in `/etc/group`. UID 0 is **root**: the kernel skips permission checks for it.
- `chown user:group file` changes ownership (only root can give files away). `chown -R` recurses. `chgrp group file` changes just the group.
- `sudo usermod -aG docker ana` adds ana to a group. **Log out and in** before it takes effect: groups are read at login.

steps.prompt: Give the web root to the `www-data` user and group, recursively.

steps.title: sudo, and why not to live as root
body: `sudo cmd` runs **one** command as root, after checking `/etc/sudoers` (edit it only with `visudo`, which refuses to save syntax errors that would lock you out).
```text
sudo systemctl restart nginx     # one privileged action
sudo -i                          # a root shell: use sparingly
sudo -u postgres psql            # run as another user
A classic trap: `sudo echo x > /etc/file` fails, because the **redirection is done by your own shell**, not by sudo. Use `echo x | sudo tee /etc/file` (or `tee -a` to append).

steps.prompt: `sudo echo "10.0.0.5 db" >> /etc/hosts` says *Permission denied*. Which fixes it?
steps.explain: `>>` is performed by your unprivileged shell before sudo runs. `tee` runs under sudo and opens the file itself. Option 2 has the same bug *and* would truncate the file.

steps.title: umask: the default permissions
body: New files start from `666` and new directories from `777`, then the **umask** bits are *removed*.
```text
umask 022       (typical)
dir:   777 & ~022 = 755   rwxr-xr-x
umask 077       (private)
file:  600      dir: 700
It's a mask, not a subtraction: each bit set in the umask is cleared. Set it in `~/.bashrc` or a service's unit file (`UMask=0027`).

steps.prompt: With `umask 027`, what permissions (as rwx) does a newly created **directory** get?
steps.explain: 777 with 027 cleared = 750. `stat -c %A` prints the type character too.

items: `chgrp` to a group the owner belongs to
steps.explain: Owners control the mode bits of their own files. Giving files to someone else, system config and ports below 1024 need root.

steps.title: umask
prompt: Write `string DefaultMode(string umask, bool isDirectory)` returning the 3-digit octal mode a new file or directory gets. `umask` is 3 or 4 octal digits (`"022"` or `"0027"`); only the last 3 matter.
Hint: parse octal with `Convert.ToInt32(s, 8)` and print with `Convert.ToString(n, 8)`, padded to 3 digits.
hints: Clear bits with `start & ~mask`, never subtract: umask 033 on a file gives 644, not 633.
